questions.question: What is the difference between `os.Getenv` and `os.LookupEnv`?
questions.title: Getenv versus LookupEnv
questions.direct_answer: `os.Getenv(key)` returns the value or an empty string, so it cannot distinguish a missing variable from one deliberately set to empty. `os.LookupEnv(key)` returns both the value and a Boolean indicating whether the key exists. Use LookupEnv whenever absent and present-but-empty have different meanings or validation messages.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Missing and present-empty both look empty through Getenv.
`found == true` can accompany an empty value.
Choose according to the configuration contract for empty values.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`os.Getenv` is the simplest environment lookup. It returns a string and uses the empty string when the key is absent. That is fine when empty and missing intentionally have the same default behaviour, but it loses one piece of state.

`os.LookupEnv` returns `value, found`. A false Boolean means the key is absent; true means the key exists even when value is empty. That distinction is important for required variables and for settings where empty explicitly disables a feature.

For example, after setting `APP_LABEL` to an empty value, Getenv returns `""` and LookupEnv returns `"", true`. After unsetting it, Getenv still returns `""` while LookupEnv returns `"", false`. Only the second API can explain the difference.

Lookup does not parse, validate, redact, or freeze configuration. After presence is known, the startup layer should decide whether empty is legal, convert typed values, and return useful errors. I use Getenv only when collapsing absent and empty is an explicit requirement rather than an accidental shortcut.

sections.title: Configuration presence and configuration value are separate facts
sections.content:
An environment entry can occupy three application states: missing, present with an empty string, or present with a non-empty string. Getenv maps the first two to one result; LookupEnv preserves all three.

The application then assigns meaning. A missing optional value may use a default, while a present-empty secret should usually fail validation. The operating-system API cannot infer that domain rule.

sections.title: Concept guide · Getenv versus LookupEnv
sections.content:
Presence is only the first check. Integers need range validation, URLs need parsing and scheme policy, durations need accepted units, and secrets need nonempty rules. A small config loader can collect these decisions in one place.

Environment variable names and values are process state. Avoid logging secrets or embedding raw values in errors. Return the variable name and the violated rule while redacting the content itself.

sections.title: The state each API can observe
sections.content:
| Environment state | `Getenv` | `LookupEnv` |
|---|---|---|
| Missing | `""` | `"", false` |
| Present, empty | `""` | `"", true` |
| Present, `prod` | `"prod"` | `"prod", true` |

questions.question: How should a Go application load and validate environment configuration?
questions.title: Loading typed configuration at startup
questions.direct_answer: Read environment values once near startup, distinguish missing from empty, parse them into a typed configuration value, validate cross-field rules, and fail with clear redacted errors before serving traffic. Pass the resulting config to components instead of scattering `os.Getenv` calls throughout business code. Injecting the lookup function also makes validation tests deterministic.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Load configuration at one startup boundary.
Parse strings into typed ports, durations, URLs, and modes.
Validate ranges and cross-field rules before starting work.
Pass an immutable config value and redact secrets from logs.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Environment variables are strings, while application configuration has types and invariants. I load them at a clear startup boundary into a struct, using LookupEnv for required presence and parsing packages such as `strconv`, `time`, and `net/url` for actual types.

Validation belongs beside loading. A port must be numeric and within 1 through 65535; a duration may need to be positive; two TLS settings may be required together. Startup should fail before listeners and workers begin, with errors that name the key and rule but do not expose secret values.

For example, a loader can turn `APP_PORT=8080` and `APP_DEBUG=true` into `Config{Port: 8080, Debug: true}`. `APP_PORT=99999` is rejected rather than silently wrapped, defaulted, or discovered only when the server tries to bind.

Reading Getenv throughout the code makes behaviour time-dependent, repeats defaults, and complicates tests. I pass the validated config to constructors. A loader that accepts a lookup function can be tested with an in-memory map, leaving global process state untouched and making missing, empty, and invalid cases explicit.

sections.title: Convert process strings into an application contract
sections.content:
The environment is an external transport for configuration, not the domain model itself. A typed struct becomes the stable internal representation and allows the compiler to protect later code from repeated string parsing.

One startup boundary also produces one error policy. Required, optional, defaulted, secret, and mutually dependent settings can be reviewed together before any partial service startup occurs.

sections.title: Concept guide · Loading typed configuration at startup
sections.content:
Lookup asks whether raw text exists. Parsing turns text into a type. Validation tests whether that typed value is permitted for this application. Construction passes the finished config to components. Keeping these stages distinct yields focused errors and tests.

Defaults should be product decisions, not consequences of a parse failure. A missing optional timeout may receive a documented default, while `"not-a-duration"` should fail rather than silently selecting that default. Secret fields should implement careful String behaviour or avoid generic struct logging.

sections.title: Startup configuration pipeline
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Process environment] --> B[Lookup required and optional keys]
  B --> C[Parse strings into types]
  C --> D[Validate ranges and relationships]
  D -->|valid| E[Immutable Config value]
  D -->|invalid| F[Redacted startup error]
  E --> G[Construct application components]
```

questions.question: Why can changing environment variables make parallel tests unreliable?
questions.title: Process-wide environment state in tests
questions.direct_answer: Environment variables belong to the entire process, not one goroutine or one test. Changing a key can alter code running concurrently and create order-dependent results. `testing.T.Setenv` restores the old value automatically, but Go forbids it in parallel tests or tests with parallel ancestors. Prefer injecting configuration or a lookup function for parallel-safe unit tests.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The process environment is shared by every goroutine.
Changing one key can interfere with concurrent tests and application code.
`t.Setenv` cannot be used in a parallel test or under a parallel ancestor.
Injected lookup functions allow independent parallel test cases.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An environment variable is process-global state. Two goroutines do not receive private copies, so a test that changes `APP_MODE` can affect another test, background goroutine, or package reading that key at the same time. The failure may depend on scheduling and disappear when run alone.

`testing.T.Setenv` is safer than raw `os.Setenv` for a sequential test because it registers cleanup that restores the previous value. The testing package explicitly disallows Setenv in parallel tests and tests with parallel ancestors because restoration cannot isolate a process-wide mutation.

For example, two config tests can each pass a separate lookup closure backed by a local map—one returns `dev` and one returns `prod`. They can run concurrently without changing the process and without relying on cleanup order.

Integration tests that truly verify environment wiring can remain sequential and use `t.Setenv`. Most parsing and validation tests should target a loader with injected raw values. That design makes dependencies visible, preserves parallelism, and avoids treating Setenv as a synchronization mechanism.

sections.title: Cleanup restores state later; it does not create isolation now
sections.content:
Automatic restoration prevents a sequential test from permanently contaminating later tests. During the test, however, the changed value is visible everywhere in the process. Concurrent readers can still observe it.

Dependency injection replaces one shared mutable namespace with per-test values. Each case controls its own lookup result, so execution order and goroutine scheduling no longer change configuration behaviour.

sections.title: Concept guide · Process-wide environment state in tests
sections.content:
A small number of sequential tests can prove that production wiring calls `os.LookupEnv`. The larger matrix—missing, empty, invalid, defaulted, and cross-field cases—can call the parsing function with local maps and run in parallel.

A mutex around Setenv calls cannot protect unrelated code that reads the environment without using the same mutex. The reliable boundary is architectural: do not mutate the shared process state for tests that only need to provide configuration values.

sections.title: Two testing strategies
sections.content:
| Strategy | Isolation | Parallel use | Best role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `t.Setenv` | Restores after test; shared during test | Forbidden with parallel test or ancestor | Small sequential wiring test |
| Injected lookup/map | Per test case | Safe when local values are not shared | Parsing and validation matrix |
| Raw `os.Setenv` | Manual restoration; shared during test | Logically unsafe | Avoid in ordinary tests |

sections.title: Run independent configuration lookups concurrently
